channel.title: Components on Gate One
channel.description: Recent content in Components on Gate One

item.title: Reverse proxy
item.description:
Gate One protects applications as a reverse proxy, but it should itself sit behind a front reverse proxy or ingress controller in most deployments (Traefik, nginx, Caddy, a cloud load balancer).

Why

  • Gate One listens on plain HTTP and does not manage certificates. The ingress terminates TLS, renews certificates and applies HSTS.

  • One public entry point gives OIDC redirect URIs, cookie domains and MCP metadata a stable URL that is independent of the container address.

  • The ingress load-balances and health-checks the Gate One replicas, so the container port never has to be published.

  • WAF rules, rate limits, request-size limits and access logs stay in front of Gate One instead of competing with its own route policy.

  • Only the ingress needs to know where Gate One runs; clients cannot reach it directly.

item.title: cladone-auth (embedded IAM)
item.description:
cladone-auth is the optional embedded IAM: a small OIDC issuer and user directory that federates external IdPs, maps their claims to a common roles/scopes/claims model and stores per-user grants. It lets you offer IdP federation and managed users without running Keycloak, Zitadel or another full IAM.

Gate One reaches it as an ordinary OIDC issuer: authProvider.type: "oidc" with issuer pointing at the IAM.

item.title: auth-bridge
item.description:
auth-bridge is the reference implementation of the HTTP bridge contract. Use it when your identity technology is not OAuth/OIDC — SAML, LDAP, mTLS, API keys, a legacy session service — or when you already run auth-bridge in front of Keycloak.

Gate One reaches it with authProvider.type: "http-bridge". The bridge owns the session; Gate One still enforces auth, auth.identity and MCP scope checks on every request.

item.title: HTTP bridge contract
item.description: authProvider.type: "http-bridge" delegates request verification to an external HTTP service: the bridge. The bridge adapts a technology Gate One does not implement natively — SAML, LDAP, mTLS, API keys, a legacy session service — to three small endpoints and a login page.

item.title: Token broker
item.description:
The token broker is the optional companion service behind Delegated credentials. It holds a registry of OAuth 2.0 providers and an encrypted per-user token store, and hands Gate One the access token of one authenticated user for one provider.

It is deliberately not an identity provider and not a reverse proxy: Gate One keeps its own identity; the broker only obtains and stores the user’s token for an upstream service.

item.title: Redis
item.description:
A single Gate One instance keeps its OIDC session and revocation state in a local bbolt file. That is enough for one instance and needs no Redis.

bbolt is local to the instance and cannot be shared safely by several Gate One replicas: a logout or a back-channel revocation recorded on one node would not be visible to the others. As soon as a second replica runs, that shared state moves to Redis.
